title: Vegas Hangover: Why It's Worse and How to Recover Fast
excerpt: Why hangovers hit harder in Las Vegas (desert air, heat, free casino drinks, little sleep), how to recover the morning after, whether IV drips are worth it, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Why Vegas hangovers hit harder: dry desert heat, free drinks, little sleep. How to recover, plan ahead, judge IV drips, and spot heat illness.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** a Vegas hangover usually hits harder than the one you get at home, and it isn't because the drinks are stronger. It's the setting. You're in a very dry desert climate, often in serious heat, drinking for longer stretches than you normally would, sleeping less, eating at odd hours, and getting handed free drinks for as long as you keep playing. Each of those makes the next morning worse, and they stack. The good news is that most of them are things you can plan around before the trip, not just treat after.

**The quick rules:** Drink a full glass of water with every alcoholic drink, and more on hot days. Eat a real meal before you start, not after. Set a drink limit before you sit down at a table, because free drinks make counting hard. Get out of the sun between pool time and night plans. Use an electrolyte drink, not just water, if you've been sweating. And know the difference between a bad hangover and heat illness or alcohol poisoning, because in Las Vegas in summer, the three can look alike.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article shares general information for adults who drink socially. **Call 911 or get to an emergency room if** someone is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has slow or irregular breathing, has a seizure, has very pale or bluish skin, or has a very high body temperature with hot, flushed skin, especially after time in the sun. Those can be signs of alcohol poisoning or heat stroke, and both are emergencies. **See a doctor if** you can't keep fluids down for most of a day, you have chest pain or a racing heartbeat that doesn't settle with rest, or you feel much worse instead of better by the afternoon.

## Why a Vegas Hangover Feels Worse Than a Normal One

A hangover is your body dealing with several things at once: dehydration and lost electrolytes, poor sleep, irritation of the stomach lining, low blood sugar, inflammation, and the after-effects of breaking down alcohol. None of that is unique to Las Vegas. What Vegas does is turn the dial up on almost every one of them at the same time.

### The desert air dries you out faster

Las Vegas sits in the Mojave Desert, and the air is very dry for most of the year. In dry air, sweat evaporates almost as soon as it forms, so you often don't feel sweaty even while you're losing a lot of water. You also lose more moisture just by breathing. Visitors from humid places often say their lips, eyes, and throat feel parched within a day. That's the same water loss happening on the inside.

Now add alcohol. Alcohol suppresses a hormone called vasopressin (also known as antidiuretic hormone), which normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it around, you pee more than you drink. In a normal setting, that's a mild problem. In the desert, it stacks on top of the water you're already losing to dry air and sweat. For a deeper look at how this works, see our guide on [whether alcohol really dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you).

### The heat is a separate problem

Summer in Las Vegas regularly brings daytime temperatures above 100°F, and nights can stay warm. Heat makes you sweat, and sweat takes sodium and potassium with it, not just water. Alcohol also widens blood vessels near the skin, which can make you feel warm and flushed and can make it harder for your body to manage heat. That's why a day at a pool party followed by a night out is a classic recipe for the worst hangover of the trip.

Heat and alcohol also blunt your judgement about both. You notice thirst less, you notice overheating less, and you're less likely to step into the shade when you should.

### Casinos are designed for long sessions

Casino floors are famous for having no clocks and few windows. Whether or not that's deliberate, the effect is real: it's easy to lose track of time, and a "couple of drinks" can quietly stretch across five or six hours. Many casinos also offer complimentary drinks to people who are gambling, which removes the natural pause of walking to the bar and paying. Every time the server comes by, it's easy to say yes.

The result is more total alcohol over a longer stretch, often without food. That's a reliable way to wake up feeling terrible.

### The schedule wrecks your sleep

Vegas trips tend to involve late nights, early pool reservations, flights at odd hours, and sometimes a time zone change. Alcohol already makes sleep worse. It can help you fall asleep, but it fragments the second half of the night and cuts into the deeper, more restorative stages. Short, broken sleep is one of the biggest drivers of how bad a hangover feels, and on a typical Vegas trip you get short, broken sleep several nights in a row. If you're lying awake at 5 a.m. with your heart pounding, our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains what's going on.

### Big, sweet, strong drinks

Vegas is known for oversized novelty drinks, yard-long frozen cocktails, and bottle service. Large frozen drinks often contain several shots of alcohol plus a lot of sugar, and it's hard to tell how much you've actually had. Sugary mixers also make it easier to drink fast, because they hide the taste of the alcohol. Darker spirits and some red wines contain more congeners, which are by-products of fermentation that some research links to worse hangovers, though the total amount of alcohol matters far more than the type.

## Hungover in Vegas: What to Do the Morning After

If you're reading this in a hotel room with the curtains closed, start here. These steps are in rough order of usefulness.

### 1. Drink fluids with electrolytes, slowly

Plain water helps, but if you've been sweating in the heat, you've lost salt too. An oral rehydration drink or electrolyte mix will usually do more than water alone. Sip steadily rather than chugging a liter, which can upset an already queasy stomach. A sports drink, an oral rehydration solution from a pharmacy, or an electrolyte powder mixed into a bottle of water all work. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers what to look for, and [electrolytes and alcohol](/never-hungover/electrolytes-and-alcohol) explains why sodium matters as much as water.

Most Strip hotels have shops on site that sell sports drinks and electrolyte packets, and there are large drugstores along the Strip. Hotel minibars charge a lot, so it's worth buying a few drinks the first day and keeping them in the room.

### 2. Eat something bland with salt and carbs

Low blood sugar adds to the shaky, weak feeling of a hangover. Toast, crackers, eggs, rice, bananas, or a simple breakfast sandwich are easier on the stomach than a giant greasy buffet plate. Salt in your food also helps you hold on to the fluid you're drinking. If you're nauseous, start small and wait a bit before eating more.

### 3. Stay cool and out of the sun

Don't head straight back to the pool. Heat plus dehydration plus a hangover is how people end up in urgent care. Give yourself a few hours somewhere air-conditioned, keep drinking fluids, and go back out once you've eaten and your urine is pale again.

### 4. Choose your painkiller carefully

If you have a headache, ibuprofen or naproxen with food is a common choice, but these can irritate a stomach that alcohol has already irritated, and they're harder on the kidneys when you're dehydrated. Acetaminophen (Tylenol) is easier on the stomach but adds work for the liver, and you shouldn't take it while alcohol is still in your system or if you drink heavily on a regular basis. Take one standard dose with water and food, not a handful, and read the label. Our [Tylenol and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol) goes into detail on safe timing.

### 5. Sleep if you can

A nap in a dark, cool room is one of the most effective hangover tools available, and Vegas hotel rooms tend to have heavy blackout curtains for exactly this reason. Put the phone on do-not-disturb and give yourself an hour or two.

### 6. Skip the "hair of the dog"

A morning Bloody Mary or mimosa at brunch can make you feel better for an hour, because it postpones the withdrawal side of the hangover. It doesn't fix anything. It just pushes the hangover later and adds more alcohol for your body to process, in the heat, on a day you were probably planning to drink again anyway.

## Vegas Hangover IV Drips: Do They Work?

Las Vegas has many IV hydration lounges and mobile services that will come to your hotel room and set up an IV of fluids, often with added vitamins and anti-nausea or pain medication. They're popular, and plenty of people say they felt better afterward.

Here's an honest view:

- **IV fluids do rehydrate you quickly.** If you're so nauseous that you can't keep anything down, getting fluids directly into a vein can help, and the anti-nausea medicine some services include can make a real difference.
- **There is no good evidence that an IV drip beats drinking fluids for a typical hangover.** If you can keep liquids down, an electrolyte drink and some food will get you most of the way there for a fraction of the cost.
- **The vitamin add-ons are mostly marketing.** There's little evidence that a vitamin infusion shortens a hangover in people who aren't deficient.
- **They aren't risk-free.** An IV is a medical procedure. There's a small risk of infection, bruising, or vein irritation, and the quality of services varies. If you use one, look for a service where a licensed nurse or medical professional places the IV and asks about your health and medications first.
- **They can't treat alcohol poisoning or heat stroke.** If someone is confused, unresponsive, or overheating, that's a 911 call, not a hotel-room drip.

We cover cost, evidence, and what to ask before booking in our full guide to [hangover IV drips](/never-hungover/hangover-iv-drip).

## Drinking in Vegas: How to Plan So You Feel Better Tomorrow

The best Vegas hangover cure is the one you set up before the first drink. None of this requires drinking less than you want to, though that helps most of all. It's about removing the extra factors that make a Vegas morning worse than a normal one.

### Before you go out

- **Eat a real meal.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream. A meal with protein, fat, and carbohydrates is better than a snack. Don't wait until midnight to eat.
- **Start hydrated.** If you've spent the afternoon in the sun, drink a couple of glasses of water or an electrolyte drink before your first cocktail. Check your urine: pale yellow is the goal.
- **Pick a number.** Decide how many drinks you'll have before you get to the table or the club. Free casino drinks and bottle service make it very hard to count after the fact.
- **Bring a bottle.** Carrying a refillable water bottle in the desert is basic sense. Many hotels have water stations or will refill on request.

Our guide on [what to take before drinking](/never-hungover/what-to-take-before-drinking) goes through which pre-drinking steps have real evidence behind them.

### While you're drinking

- **Alternate.** Have a glass of water between every alcoholic drink. On a hot day or a dance floor, make it a bigger glass. Bartenders and cocktail servers will bring water if you ask.
- **Watch the giant drinks.** A single yard-long frozen cocktail or a big souvenir cup can hold as much alcohol as several normal drinks. Treat it as several drinks, not one.
- **Slow the free drinks.** When you're gambling, it's fine to order a water or a soda when the server comes by. Tipping for water is a nice gesture and keeps the server coming back.
- **Go clear and simple when you can.** Spirits with soda water and lime, or a light beer, are easier to pace than sugary frozen drinks. The type matters less than the amount, but simpler drinks make it easier to keep count.
- **Take breaks outside the casino.** Step out, look at the sky, check the time. It resets your sense of how long you've been going.

### Pool days and dayclubs

Pool parties are where Vegas hangovers often begin. You're drinking in direct sun, sweating, often not eating much, and sometimes starting before noon.

- **Eat before you go,** and order food at the pool.
- **Drink water at least as often as you drink alcohol,** and more in the afternoon heat.
- **Use shade and sunscreen.** A sunburn adds inflammation and makes you feel worse the next day.
- **Get out and cool down** between the pool and dinner. A shower and an hour in the air conditioning before going out again makes a real difference.
- **Watch your friends.** Heat illness and too much alcohol can come on together, and the person affected is usually the last to notice.

### Before bed

- **Drink a large glass of water or an electrolyte drink.** Keep another one on the nightstand.
- **Eat something small** if you haven't eaten in several hours.
- **Skip sleep aids.** Combining alcohol with sedating medicines such as diphenhydramine (the ingredient in many "PM" products) increases drowsiness and impairment.
- **Set the room cool and dark.** Most Vegas rooms make this easy.

### Across a multi-day trip

Hangovers compound. If you drink heavily on Friday and wake up dehydrated and short on sleep, Saturday night hits harder. A few habits help:

- Plan at least one lighter night, especially before a big event.
- Keep a supply of electrolyte drinks in the room from day one.
- Eat breakfast every day, even if it's late.
- Schedule things you actually want to do in the morning on the day after your lightest night, not your heaviest.

If you're traveling with a group for a bachelor or bachelorette party, our [party drinking tips](/never-hungover/party-drinking-tips) and [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) guides have more on pacing over a long weekend.

## What to Pack for a Vegas Trip

A small kit saves money and a bad morning. Hotel shops are convenient, but prices on the Strip are high. For more ideas, see our [hangover kit ideas](/never-hungover/hangover-kit-ideas).

| Item | Why it helps |
|---|---|
| Refillable water bottle | Makes it easy to keep drinking water in dry heat |
| Electrolyte powder or packets | Replaces sodium and potassium lost to sweat and alcohol |
| A pain reliever you know you tolerate | So you're not guessing at a strange brand at 3 a.m.; follow the label |
| Antacid | For the heartburn and upset stomach that often follow a big night |
| Sunscreen, sunglasses, a hat | Sunburn and glare add to how bad you feel |
| Lip balm and eye drops | Desert air dries both out quickly |
| Small snacks | Crackers or nuts for the late night and the early morning |
| Earplugs and an eye mask | Better sleep in a loud hotel or on a shared floor |

## Hangover, Heat Illness, or Alcohol Poisoning? How to Tell

This is the most important section of this article. In Las Vegas, especially between May and September, the symptoms of a bad hangover, heat exhaustion, heat stroke, and alcohol poisoning can overlap. Some of these are emergencies.

### A normal hangover

Headache, tiredness, nausea, thirst, sensitivity to light and noise, poor concentration, and a general unwell feeling. It's unpleasant but it gets better over the day with fluids, food, rest, and time. The person is awake, can talk normally, and knows where they are.

### Heat exhaustion

Heavy sweating, cool and clammy skin, weakness, dizziness, headache, nausea or vomiting, muscle cramps, and a fast but weak pulse. **What to do:** move to a cool place, loosen clothing, apply cool wet cloths, and sip water or an electrolyte drink. Get medical help if the person is vomiting, if symptoms get worse, or if they don't improve within about an hour.

### Heat stroke (emergency)

A very high body temperature, hot skin that may be red and either dry or damp, a fast strong pulse, confusion, slurred speech, fainting, or seizures. **Call 911 right away.** While waiting, move the person somewhere cool and cool them down with water, wet cloths, or ice packs on the neck, armpits, and groin. Don't give fluids to someone who is confused or not fully awake. Heat stroke can cause lasting damage or death, and alcohol can make it harder to recognize because confusion gets blamed on being drunk.

### Alcohol poisoning (emergency)

Confusion, being unable to wake up or stay awake, vomiting repeatedly, seizures, slow breathing (fewer than eight breaths a minute) or long gaps between breaths, pale or bluish skin, and a low body temperature. **Call 911 right away.** Don't let them "sleep it off." Keep them on their side so they won't choke if they vomit, and stay with them. Our guide to the [signs of alcohol poisoning](/never-hungover/alcohol-poisoning-signs) explains the difference in more detail.

A useful rule in Vegas: **if someone is confused or can't be woken, it's not your job to figure out whether it's the heat or the alcohol.** Either way, call 911. Paramedics deal with this every day on the Strip, and getting help fast matters far more than avoiding an awkward moment.

### Other signs that need a doctor

- You can't keep fluids down for most of a day
- Your heart is racing or skipping and doesn't calm down with rest and fluids (see [heart racing after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking))
- Chest pain, severe stomach pain, or vomiting blood
- Shaking, sweating, and anxiety that keep getting worse over a day or two after a long stretch of heavy drinking, which can be an early sign of alcohol withdrawal and is worth getting checked by a doctor rather than waiting it out

## Medications and Vegas Drinking

If you take prescription medication, check whether it interacts with alcohol before the trip, not at the bar. Common examples that don't mix well with alcohol include some antidepressants, anti-anxiety medicines, sleep aids, opioid painkillers, some antibiotics such as metronidazole, and diabetes medicines that can cause low blood sugar. Some medicines also make you more sensitive to heat or sun. A quick question to your pharmacist before you fly is the easiest way to find out. If a medicine says "avoid alcohol" on the label, take that seriously in Vegas, where the drinking sessions tend to be longer than at home.

## Myths About Curing a Vegas Hangover

- **"Sweating it out in the sauna or steam room helps."** It doesn't speed up how fast your body clears alcohol, and it makes dehydration worse. In the desert, after a night of drinking, a hot room is a bad idea.
- **"A big greasy breakfast soaks up the alcohol."** Food before drinking slows alcohol absorption. Food the next morning helps with blood sugar and energy, but it doesn't soak up alcohol that's already been absorbed.
- **"Coffee cures a hangover."** Caffeine can help with grogginess and a caffeine-withdrawal headache, but it doesn't fix dehydration. Pair it with water.
- **"Oxygen bars fix hangovers."** Some Vegas venues offer flavored oxygen. There is no good evidence that it helps a hangover in a healthy person.
- **"An IV is the only thing that works."** For most hangovers, oral fluids, food, rest, and time work too, at a far lower cost.

## Where DHM Fits In

Some people add a DHM supplement to their Vegas plans. DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a compound from the Japanese raisin tree that has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the evidence comes from animal and lab studies, with only limited human data. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people, and it doesn't replace water, food, sleep, or pacing yourself, which matter far more in desert heat. It also won't protect you from heat illness or alcohol poisoning.

If you want to try it as one part of your plan, people usually take it with a glass of water during or after drinking. Popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20), which are easy to pack in a carry-on. Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much to take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands. If you take prescription medication, check with your pharmacist before adding any supplement.

## The Bottom Line

- A Vegas hangover is usually worse because of the setting: dry desert air, heat, long drinking sessions, free drinks, little sleep, and irregular meals.
- Most of that is fixable with planning: eat first, set a drink limit, alternate every drink with water, use electrolytes, and take breaks from the sun and the casino floor.
- The morning after, sip electrolyte fluids, eat something bland, stay cool, take a single standard dose of a painkiller with food if you need one, and sleep.
- IV drips can help if you can't keep fluids down, but there is no good evidence they beat drinking fluids for a typical hangover.
- Know the emergency signs. Confusion, being hard to wake, repeated vomiting, slow breathing, or a very high temperature means call 911, whether you think it's the heat or the alcohol.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why are hangovers worse in Vegas?**

Las Vegas combines several things that make hangovers worse at the same time. The desert air is very dry and summers are very hot, so you lose more water than you notice. Casinos make it easy to drink for hours, often with free drinks and no clocks, and Vegas trips usually involve late nights, short sleep, and irregular meals. Alcohol itself makes you lose water and disrupts sleep, so the setting magnifies its effects.

**What's the best way to cure a hangover in Vegas?**

There's no instant cure, but the most helpful steps are sipping an electrolyte drink or oral rehydration solution, eating something bland with salt and carbohydrates, staying out of the heat in an air-conditioned room, taking a single standard dose of a pain reliever with food if you need one, and sleeping. Avoid the sauna and the "hair of the dog," which make things worse. Most hangovers improve over the day.

**Are Vegas hangover IV drips worth it?**

They can help if you're too nauseous to keep fluids down, especially if anti-nausea medicine is included. For a typical hangover, there's no good evidence that an IV works better than drinking fluids and eating, and the vitamin add-ons are mostly marketing. If you book one, choose a service where a licensed medical professional places the IV and reviews your health and medications first. An IV is not a substitute for emergency care.

**How much water should I drink in Vegas if I'm drinking alcohol?**

There's no exact number that fits everyone, because it depends on your size, the heat, and how active you are. A practical rule is to drink at least one glass of water for every alcoholic drink, more on hot days or when you're dancing or at a pool, and to keep your urine pale yellow. In the heat, add an electrolyte drink rather than relying on water alone.

**Are the free drinks in Vegas casinos stronger?**

There's no reliable evidence that casino drinks are stronger than drinks elsewhere, and pours vary a lot by venue. The bigger issue is volume: free drinks while gambling remove the natural pause of paying, the sessions are long, and it's easy to lose count. Decide on a number before you sit down, and order water or soda between drinks.

**How can I tell if it's heat exhaustion or a hangover?**

They overlap: both can cause headache, nausea, weakness, and dizziness. Heat exhaustion usually follows time in the sun and comes with heavy sweating, cool clammy skin, and muscle cramps. Move to a cool place and sip fluids, and get medical help if it doesn't improve within about an hour. Confusion, a very high temperature, hot skin, or fainting can mean heat stroke, which needs 911 right away.

**When should I go to the ER after drinking in Vegas?**

Call 911 or go to the emergency room if someone is confused, can't be woken or stay awake, is vomiting repeatedly, has a seizure, has slow or irregular breathing, has pale or bluish skin, or has a very high body temperature after time in the sun. See a doctor if you can't keep fluids down for most of a day or have chest pain or a racing heart that won't settle.

**Does DHM help with a Vegas hangover?**

DHM has been studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism, mostly in animal and lab research, with limited human data. There is no good evidence that it prevents hangovers in people, and it won't protect you from dehydration, heat illness, or alcohol poisoning. Some people use it as one part of their plan, but water, food, sleep, and pacing matter far more in the desert.
